rows.grounds: instruments and qualities such as aṇimā
sattva and the rest belonging to them

items.question: What arises from the unmanifest in this account of the worlds?
premises: The organs and subtle powers such as aṇimā are listed as products.
Effects and the expansion of cognitions are also listed as products.
The qualities sattva and the others arise from the unmanifest.
items.inference: The unmanifest is the source of instruments, powers, effects, cognitions, and the guṇas.
uncertainties: The exact scope of pratyayaprapañca in this cosmological context is somewhat compressed.
items.plain_english: From the unmanifest arise the organs, the subtle powers like smallness, the effects, the manifold of cognitions, and the qualities beginning with sattva.

rows.grounds: the four qualities dharma, jñāna, virāga, aiśvarya

items.question: What do the givers of yoga bestow upon the souls?
premises: The givers of yoga arise from the guṇas.
They bestow merit, knowledge, dispassion, and lordship.
They also bestow the various fruits of those qualities.
items.inference: Beings arising from the guṇas act as givers of yoga by granting spiritual qualities and their results to souls.
uncertainties: The precise referent of yogadātāraḥ depends on the immediately preceding context.
items.plain_english: These givers of yoga, arising from the qualities, bestow on souls merit, knowledge, dispassion, lordship, and their various fruits.

rows.grounds: of the deity whose seat is the guṇas beginning with sattva
of the lord who is the consort of the sole mother of the entire universe

items.question: Which world lies beyond those givers of yoga?
premises: Beyond those beings there is a higher world.
That world belongs to the deity seated on the guṇas beginning with sattva.
That deity is Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, lord and consort of the one mother of the whole universe.
items.inference: The next world in the hierarchy is the world of Śrīkaṇṭhanātha.
uncertainties: The compound sakalajagadekamāturbhartuḥ can be read with slight variation in relational nuance.
items.plain_english: Beyond them is the world of the god Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, who is seated on the qualities beginning with sattva and is the lord and consort of the one mother of the entire universe.

rows.grounds: by whom, in the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣa, Kṛta, Akṛta, and others
in the form of a graha or seizing power
ruling over Prabhū and other beings

items.question: How does Śrīkaṇṭha exercise power over the beings in those worlds?
premises: Śrīkaṇṭha acts in the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣa, Kṛta, Akṛta, and others.
He acts through a śakti that takes a seizing or governing form.
Through that śakti he presides over the beings there.
items.inference: Śrīkaṇṭha governs the inhabitants of those worlds by means of his śakti.
uncertainties: graharūpiṇyā may suggest a seizing, planetary, or controlling form; the exact nuance is interpretive.
items.plain_english: By his power, taking a seizing form, he presides over the beings in the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣa, Kṛta, Akṛta, and others.

rows.grounds: who, entering the lotus of the four-faced Brahmā
burns the four worlds and again creates the worlds of people

items.question: What cosmic action is performed when reabsorption and creation occur?
premises: The deity desires to withdraw the worlds.
He enters the lotus of the four-faced Brahmā and burns the four worlds.
After burning them, he creates the worlds of people again.
items.inference: The same divine agency governs both dissolution and renewed creation of the worlds.
uncertainties: The exact identity of the four worlds is not specified in this verse alone.
items.plain_english: When he wishes to withdraw the worlds, he enters the lotus of the four-faced Brahmā, burns the four worlds, and then creates the human worlds again.

rows.grounds: whose body consists of the guṇas beginning with sattva
there she is worshiped in every cycle

items.question: What role does Rudrāṇī play in the cyclical activity described here?
premises: Rudrāṇī, whose body is made of the guṇas beginning with sattva, acts by the deity's will.
She emits or brings forth in each cycle.
She is worshiped at the altar in each cycle.
items.inference: Rudrāṇī functions as a cyclical creative and ritual power under the deity's will.
uncertainties: The object of visṛjati is not explicitly stated in this verse.
items.plain_english: By his will, Rudrāṇī, whose body consists of the qualities beginning with sattva, brings forth in each cycle, and there she is worshiped at the altar in every cycle.

rows.grounds: then by Paśupati, Indra, Upendra, and Viriñci
and likewise varied rites are performed by gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, and sages

items.question: Who performs the varied sacrifices connected with that attainment?
premises: Paśupati, Indra, Upendra, and Viriñci are involved in that attainment.
The gods receive or participate in it.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, and sages perform varied sacrifices.
items.inference: A wide range of divine and semi-divine beings perform ritual worship in connection with that attainment.
uncertainties: The exact referent of tad in tadupalambhataḥ is carried over from the previous verse.
items.plain_english: Then, in connection with that attainment, Paśupati, Indra, Upendra, Viriñci, the gods, and also gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, and sages perform varied sacrifices.

rows.grounds: the deities Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, and Saṃvarta

items.question: What is identified as the unmanifest above the level of the guṇas?
premises: The supreme equilibrium of the guṇas is called the unmanifest.
This unmanifest is located above the guṇa level.
Deities such as Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotiḥ, Piṅgala, and Sūraka are associated there.
items.inference: The balanced state of the guṇas is the unmanifest principle situated above the guṇa realm and populated by specific deities.
uncertainties: The final compound lists several names whose exact grouping as dual or plural is compressed in transmission.
items.plain_english: The supreme equilibrium of the qualities is the unmanifest. Above the level of the qualities are Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotiḥ, Piṅgala, and Sūraka.

items.question: How is the unmanifest principle characterized in this world-group?
premises: Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and Śikhin complete a group of eight there.
That principle is described as dense and as the resting place of the puruṣa.
It is identified as prakṛti, the root, pradhāna, and the unmanifest.
items.inference: The unmanifest is presented as the foundational material principle in which the puruṣa rests.
uncertainties: The count of eight depends on combining names from this and the previous verse.
items.plain_english: There are Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and Śikhin, making eight. There that principle is the dense resting place of the soul, prakṛti, the root, pradhāna, the unmanifest.

rows.grounds: thus these are called the cause of the guṇas
of that which is born from māyā
whose minds are tainted by both innate and adventitious impurity

items.question: Who are said to be present in relation to the māyā-born unmanifest?
premises: The unmanifest is described by several synonymous names as the cause of the guṇas.
It belongs to the domain arising from māyā.
All embodied knowers whose minds are stained by innate and adventitious impurity are associated with it.
items.inference: The māyā-born unmanifest is the locus associated with all impure embodied knowers.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically compressed and continues into the next verse.
items.plain_english: These are synonymous names for the cause of the qualities, belonging to what arises from māyā; all the embodied knowers whose minds are stained by innate and adventitious impurity are there.

rows.grounds: those who enjoy the experiences arising from it
with faculties that are deluded, manifest, or dissolved

items.question: In what different conditions are beings situated in that realm?
premises: All those embodied knowers are established there.
Rudras there enjoy experiences arising from that principle.
Some beings have faculties that are deluded, manifest, or dissolved, while some are without faculties.
items.inference: That realm contains beings in multiple experiential conditions, including those with impaired or absent faculties.
uncertainties: The technical distinction among mūḍha, vivṛtta, and vilīna faculties is only briefly indicated.
items.plain_english: All of them are established there, along with Rudras who enjoy the experiences arising from it. Some have faculties that are deluded, manifest, or dissolved, while others are without faculties.

rows.grounds: due to not having been brought under presiding control

items.question: How are deluded and unfolded faculties distinguished in the teaching?
premises: Faculties not yet brought under presiding control are incapable of action and are called deluded.
Faculties that grasp their fixed objects clearly are called unfolded.
This distinction is stated in the teaching.
items.inference: The text distinguishes inert, ungoverned faculties from manifest faculties that function on fixed objects.
uncertainties: The subject is implicitly the faculties mentioned in the previous verse.
items.plain_english: In the teaching, faculties that are not yet governed and cannot act are called deluded, while those that clearly grasp their fixed objects are called unfolded.

rows.grounds: at the time of universal dissolution
and the effect is to be understood in the same way

items.question: When are faculties described as dissolved or without faculties?
premises: At great dissolution the faculties are broken and dissolved.
At creation they are not yet produced and remain dependent on will.
In that condition they are again called without faculties, and the same applies to their effects.
items.inference: The absence or latency of faculties is explained by cosmic dissolution, pre-creation latency, and dependence on divine will.
uncertainties: The verse compresses several temporal states into a single classificatory statement.
items.plain_english: At the great dissolution they are broken and dissolved; at creation they are not yet produced. Dependent on will, they are again called without faculties, and the same is true of their effects.

rows.grounds: at the level of the puruṣa tattva
prior to that or in front of that
just the eight worlds beginning with aṇimā

items.question: What groups are located at the level of the puruṣa principle?
premises: At the puruṣa principle there is a ninefold group of satisfactions.
There are also eight accomplishments.
There are likewise eight worlds beginning with aṇimā.
items.inference: The puruṣa level is organized into corresponding sets of satisfactions, accomplishments, and worlds.
uncertainties: The phrase tatpuraḥ is brief and may indicate sequence or relative position.
items.plain_english: At the level of the puruṣa principle there are the nine satisfactions, the eight accomplishments, and likewise the eight worlds beginning with aṇimā.

rows.grounds: in what is not truly the tattva
through the cognition that it is a tattva
a cognition of acceptability even in what should be rejected

items.question: How are satisfaction and accomplishment defined in this mistaken cognition?
premises: Taking what is not the true principle to be a principle produces a kind of contentment.
That contentment is called satisfaction here.
Taking what should be rejected as acceptable is called accomplishment, as stated by the Kāpilas.
items.inference: In this framework, both satisfaction and accomplishment can arise from misidentification.
uncertainties: The verse reports a Kāpilā view; its degree of endorsement in this text is contextual.
items.plain_english: When what is not the true principle is taken as a principle, the resulting contentment is called satisfaction. Taking what should be rejected as acceptable is called accomplishment, as the Kāpilas say.

rows.grounds: called prakṛti, upādāna, kāla, and bhāgya
five arise from cessation regarding objects through gain, protection, association, loss, and obstruction

items.question: How are the nine satisfactions classified in this account?
premises: Four satisfactions are internal.
Those four are named prakṛti, upādāna, kāla, and bhāgya.
Five satisfactions arise from cessation regarding objects through gain, protection, association, loss, and obstruction.
items.inference: The nine satisfactions are divided into four internal and five object-related forms.
uncertainties: The compressed compound for the five external causes allows slight variation in unpacking.
items.plain_english: Four satisfactions are internal, named prakṛti, acquisition, time, and fortune. Five arise from turning away from objects through gain, protection, association, loss, and obstruction.

rows.grounds: the earlier obstacle to accomplishment is threefold

items.question: What are the eight accomplishments and their threefold obstacle?
premises: Reasoning, verbal testimony, and study are three accomplishments that remove suffering.
Gaining friends and giving are also counted among the accomplishments.
The obstacle prior to accomplishment is said to be threefold.
items.inference: The eight accomplishments include cognitive, social, and remedial means, and they are opposed by a threefold hindrance.
uncertainties: The exact unpacking of the threefold aṅkuśa is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: Reasoning, scriptural word, and study are three means that remove suffering; gaining friends and giving are also included, making the eight accomplishments. The obstacle before accomplishment is threefold.

rows.grounds: above aṇimā and the rest there are three
because of association with the reflection of the three guṇas

items.question: Why are three rows said to exist above the aṇimā group?
premises: Above the worlds beginning with aṇimā there are three rows.
These rows pertain to teacher and disciple.
Their threefoldness is explained by association with the shadow of the three guṇas.
items.inference: The triadic structure of those higher rows reflects the influence of the three guṇas.
uncertainties: The term paṅkti may refer to series, channels, or grouped worlds depending on context.
items.plain_english: Above the worlds beginning with aṇimā there are three rows connected with teacher and disciple. Their threefold division is explained by the influence of the three qualities.

rows.grounds: beginning with iḍā and so on

items.question: What power is said to be established in the soul above those rows?
premises: Above the rows there is an eightfold set of nāḍī-vidyās beginning with iḍā.
In the puruṣa a śakti consisting of nāda is established.
That śakti is called prasara, expansion.
items.inference: The higher arrangement culminates in a nāda-based expansive power situated in the puruṣa.
uncertainties: The relation between nāḍīvidyāṣṭaka and the nāda-śakti is stated compactly.
items.plain_english: Above those rows is the eightfold set of nāḍī-knowledges beginning with iḍā. In the soul there is established a power made of sound, called expansion.

rows.grounds: for one who is not an agent
the puruṣa cannot have the status of an agent
the state of being a cause

items.question: Can a non-agent soul still be related to causality?
premises: A non-agent soul cannot be established as the primary doer.
Even if the soul is not an agent, it may be situated as a concomitant cause.
Causality must therefore be explained without making the soul an independent doer.
items.inference: The soul's causal role, if any, is only auxiliary rather than primary agency.
uncertainties: The argument is compressed and continues into the next verse.
items.plain_english: A soul that is not an agent cannot truly be established as the doer. Even if the soul is not an agent, it may still stand as an assisting cause.

rows.grounds: otherwise one would have to accept that it becomes the rest of the effect
since that would negate the doctrine that the effect pre-exists

items.question: Why must a special power of the soul be posited in such effects?
premises: If the soul were made part of the effect in another way, the satkārya doctrine would be undermined.
Therefore, in such an effect, a specific power of the soul must be acknowledged.
That power explains the soul's relation without reducing it to the effect.
items.inference: A distinct śakti of the puruṣa is required to preserve causal coherence and the satkārya principle.
uncertainties: The sentence completes its thought in the next verse.
items.plain_english: Otherwise one would have to treat the soul as part of the effect, which would undermine the doctrine that the effect pre-exists. Therefore, in such a case, there is a specific power belonging to the soul.

rows.grounds: the eightfold set of forms is now spoken of

items.question: What happens to the soul's power above the eight nāḍīs?
premises: The soul's power assumes as many corresponding forms.
By assuming those forms it attains fullness.
Above the eight nāḍīs an eightfold set of forms is taught.
items.inference: The expansive power of the soul becomes complete by manifesting as an eightfold set of forms above the nāḍīs.
uncertainties: The exact nature of the eight forms is explained in the following verses.
items.plain_english: Taking on that many forms, that power attains fullness. Above the eight nāḍīs, an eightfold set of forms is taught.

rows.grounds: what is to be done or produced
knowledge and the instruments that accomplish it
the eightfold set in the form of embodied pairs
at the level of the puruṣa tattva

items.question: What constitutes the eightfold set of forms at the puruṣa level?
premises: Effect, cause, suffering, and pleasure are included.
Knowledge, what is to be accomplished, instruments, and means are included.
Together these form an eightfold embodied set at the puruṣa principle.
items.inference: The puruṣa level is structured by an eightfold set of experiential and instrumental factors.
uncertainties: The compound vigrahatāyugaṣṭakaṃ is terse and may reflect a technical classificatory pairing.
items.plain_english: At the level of the puruṣa principle there is an eightfold embodied set: effect, cause, suffering, pleasure, knowledge, what is to be accomplished, the instruments, and the means.

rows.grounds: of the bodily observances or qualities
brahmacarya, absence of deceit, and absence of anger

items.question: What follows the eightfold forms in the next world-group?
premises: Beyond the eightfold forms comes the world of the ten bodily observances.
These observances include non-harm, truth, and non-stealing.
They also include continence, freedom from deceit, freedom from anger, and observances related to the teacher.
items.inference: The next cosmological grouping is defined by ten ethical-bodily disciplines.
uncertainties: The verse lists only part of the ten observances; the rest continue in the next verse.
items.plain_english: Beyond the eightfold forms is the world of the ten bodily observances: non-harm, truth, non-stealing, continence, freedom from deceit, freedom from anger, and duties toward the teacher.
